title: One editor session
caption: How a keystroke in VS Code becomes native diagnostics, quick fixes, and formatting without any extension fighting over your file type.

nodes.buffer: Everything runs on the in-memory buffer you are typing in. Unsaved changes are analyzed live, and code actions never touch disk.
nodes.framework: Your framework extension keeps its language ID, grammar, completions, and compilation. The companion registers no competing .tsrx language.
nodes.companion: The companion only attaches to file-backed .tsrx documents, launches the Rust server, and forwards workspace settings. Rust owns everything else.
nodes.server: One long-lived native process per workspace. It parses, lints, formats, maps sources, and validates fixes.
nodes.oxc: Canonical OXC parses the projected TSX copy exactly once per change, then Oxlint rules and Oxfmt layout run on that single parse.
nodes.tsgo: Type-aware and type-check diagnostics start one TypeScript-Go process only when you opt in through settings.
nodes.diagnostics: Every diagnostic maps back to the exact TSRX you typed. On the recorded machine, open to first diagnostics measured 2.40 ms median.
nodes.edits: A quick fix or format edit applies only with an exact authored mapping and a clean reparse. Malformed input returns no edit instead of a guess.

steps.label: Attach
steps.caption: You open a .tsrx file. Your framework extension keeps owning the language while the companion quietly starts the native server.

steps.label: Diagnose
steps.caption: Each edit flows to the native server, OXC parses the projection once, and squiggles land on your authored bytes in milliseconds.

steps.label: Fix and format
steps.caption: Quick fixes and format-on-save are validated against your authored bytes before the editor applies them. No valid mapping, no edit.

steps.label: Opt into types
steps.caption: Turning on oxcTsrx.typeAware or oxcTsrx.typeCheck adds TypeScript-Go diagnostics through the same authored-byte mapping.
